title: Sparse Matrix Multiplication
statement:
You get two integer matrices: `mat1` has `m` rows and `k` columns, and `mat2` has `k` rows and `n` columns. Both are sparse, meaning most of their entries are zero. Return the matrix product `mat1 × mat2`: an `m` by `n` matrix whose entry at row `i`, column `j` equals the sum of `mat1[i][p] * mat2[p][j]` over every `p` from `0` to `k - 1`.

The number of columns of `mat1` always matches the number of rows of `mat2`, so the product is always defined.
notes:
## Intuition

The plain definition computes every `result[i][j]` as a dot product of row `i` of `mat1` with column `j` of `mat2`, which always costs `m · k · n` multiplications even when almost all of them are `0 · something`. Turn the sum around: `mat1[i][p]` contributes `mat1[i][p] * mat2[p][j]` to every `j` of row `i`. If `mat1[i][p]` is zero, that whole contribution vanishes, and if `mat2[p][j]` is zero, only that one term vanishes. So only pairs of non-zero entries ever need multiplying.

## Approach

1. Read the sizes `m`, `k` and `n`.
2. For each row `p` of `mat2`, collect its non-zero entries as `[j, value]` pairs in `nonZero[p]`.
3. Start `result` as an `m` by `n` matrix of zeros.
4. For each row `i` and each `p`, take `factor = mat1[i][p]`; skip it when it is zero.
5. Otherwise add `factor * value` to `result[i][j]` for every pair `[j, value]` in `nonZero[p]`.
6. Return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nonZero` is `[[[0, 7]], [], [[2, 1]]]`. Row `i = 0` of `mat1` is `[1, 0, 0]`: only `p = 0` has a non-zero `factor = 1`, which adds `1 * 7` to `result[0][0]`. Row `i = 1` is `[-1, 0, 3]`: `p = 0` adds `-1 * 7 = -7` to `result[1][0]`, `p = 1` is skipped, and `p = 2` adds `3 * 1 = 3` to `result[1][2]`. The answer is `[[7, 0, 0], [-7, 0, 3]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(k · n + m · n + m · k + Z), where Z is the number of non-zero pairs multiplied; at worst (dense input) O(m · k · n).
- Space: O(m · n) for `result` plus the non-zero entries of `mat2`.

## Pitfalls

- The result has `m` rows and `n` columns; `n` is the width of `mat2`, not of `mat1`.
- Accumulate with `+=`: several `p` values add into the same `result[i][j]`.
- Skipping a zero must skip only that `p`, not the rest of the row (`continue`, not `break`).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `m`, `k`, `n` | rows of `mat1`, the shared inner size, columns of `mat2` |
| `nonZero[p]` | the `[j, value]` pairs of row `p` of `mat2` that are not zero |
| `result` | the product being built, `m` by `n` |
| `i`, `p` | the current row of `mat1` and the column inside it |
| `factor` | `mat1[i][p]`, the entry being spread across row `i` |
| `j`, `value` | a column of `mat2` and its non-zero entry in row `p` |
